Where we live: some dilemmas and technical issues for the child psychotherapist in interpretative work with looked-after and adopted children

Jenny Kenrick

Jenny Kenrick

Jenny Kenrick  

Looked-after and adopted children, transference, countertransference, interpretation, process interpretation, past in the present

This paper addresses, from a Kleinian perspective, some of the dilemmas and technical issues faced by the child psychotherapist in work with looked-after and adopted children. A selective review of psychoanalytic literature focusing on the use of transference and countertransference is given. Clinical material provides some examples of different kinds of interpretation, and of the importance of timing and emotional resonance in the interpretations.

Diana Cant

Diana Cant  

Child psychotherapy, sexual abuse, therapeutic community, foster-care, transitions, transitional space

This paper looks at the role of individual psychotherapy with a severely sexually abused girl in a therapeutic community, and the place of this work as she makes the transition into foster-care. It emphasizes the importance, not only of the individual work, but also of the drawing together of the work around the child, particularly at such a critical time. There is discussion of the ideas of ‘deadness’ versus ‘aliveness’ in the therapy, and detailed case material is used.

Christopher Reeves

Christopher Reeves

Gorseacre
West Polberro
St. Agnes
Cornwall TR5 OST

Christopher Reeves  

Clare Winnicott is best remembered within the psychoanalytic world as the wife of her more renowned husband Donald, in her widowhood as a staunch, sometimes ruthless, guardian of his legacy, and in her final years as a capable, if not especially original, analyst. Latterly, with the publication first of Kahr's (1996) monograph of Winnicott, and then of Rodman's more recent and fuller biography (2003), interest has focussed on Clare's role as her husband's partner and in some sense the manager of his practical affairs. Particular attention, some of it critical, has been directed at her early wartime involvement with Donald and at assessing her part in the breakdown of his first marriage. An undoubted spur to this was the virtual suppression of information about his first wife in earlier accounts of Winnicott's life and development, including notably her own, information that is now slowly beginning to emerge. All of which has served to counterbalance the earlier idyllic, if somewhat colourless, portrait of her as efficient but self-effacing, a foil to her more effervescent husband.

In spite of this recent re-evaluation of her role as Winnicott's wife, Clare herself has remained surprisingly elusive. Almost unknown, even to those with more than a passing interest in her husband's work, is the fact that she was a significant figure in public life, a true pioneer of the social work profession, a notable lecturer and administrator, and perhaps most relevant of all, an important theorist of family casework and communication with children whose views carried great weight during the third quarter of the 20th century.

This, therefore, is a timely book. It seeks to portray Clare Winnicott as a figure in her own right. In doing so, it largely avoids gossip and conjecture about the personal dimension of her relationship with Winnicott before their marriage and about her interactions with the fractious Winnicott confraternity that survived him. Instead, it comprises a clear portrayal of Clare Winnicott's early background and later professional career, partly through her own writings, and partly through the reminiscences of others. Bowlby's biographer, Jeremy Holmes, contributes a thoughtful introduction. This is followed by a biographical chapter by Kanter, a substantial piece, comprising a third of the book, and more in the nature of a short monograph. After it comes a varied selection of Clare's papers and lecture transcripts spanning her different personal and professional interests, as social work innovator, social policy adviser and psychoanalyst, and, not least, as her late husband's memorialist.

Maggie arrives bringing with her a sense of burden to which the therapist is receptive. She seems full up with worries about Steven. The therapist offers a space where the weight of her burden can be rested. Reports from school and daily struggles with Steven contribute to the sense of her exhaustion and depletion of internal resources. Perhaps the reports and the struggles are related. The sense of persecution the reports evoke in her undermines her confidence in relating to and managing Steven. Graham Music  

As the title suggests, this book attempts to bring together and make links between ideas from such diverse fields as psychoanalytic thinking (primarily from the Anna Freudian tradition), attachment theory, developmental psychology and neuroscience. Many of us in the last few years have

263

been struck by the potential importance of new theoretical ideas that the above and other related disciplines have spawned, and many clinicians have struggled with questions such as: exactly what use can we make of these ideas? How might they influence the way we think and work? Can there be some kind of synthesis of such ideas that does not seem unwieldy? Can such a synthesis retain the core values of psychoanalytic thinking yet simultaneously spearhead a re-conceptualization of some of the ways we think and work? These are complex issues, and this book, I think, goes some way towards asking the right questions, but it may be that we are as yet quite far from finding satisfactory answers to them. The editor's task is perhaps made the more difficult by the inevitable time-lag between the original conceptualization of this book, which must have been some years ago when the initial excitement about these ideas was taking root, and the eventual writing and then publishing of the papers. Ideas that were startlingly new and exciting then become, by the time a review is published, almost part of how we all think.

The book has contributions from 10 different authors, as well as an introductory chapter by Viviane Green, and these chapters are basically in two sections; in Part One there are four theoretical papers by Allan Schore, Oliver Turnbull and Mark Solms, Miriam Steele and Peter Fonagy. These chapters outline some of the central ideas emerging from the relevant neuroscience and attachment theory literature, which have influenced the way we think about clinical work. The second section contains six chapters by different therapists focussing on clinical work with a range of ages and issues, each hoping to make some link between the clinical exposition and the theoretical ideas elaborated in the first part of the book.

Sandra Ramsden  

This book is a specialist volume, which has been edited and written by experts in assessment in complex child care court cases. It is both a complement and a companion to an earlier book Assessment of Parenting, Psychiatric and Psychological Contributions, edited by P. Reder and C. Lucey, which was published in 1995. Both books have been a response to change and to need. The Children Act of 1989 and its implementation in 1991 was the initial and greatest change. The first book made contributions on both the theory and practice of assessments in family proceedings. The second embraces advances in knowledge about parenting breakdown, a variety of guidance that has been provided upon professional response to such breakdown and the testing of methods of assessment. It also addresses new questions that have arisen since the publication of the first volume.

Fourteen authors contribute seventeen chapters, which are organized in five sections. Of the preponderance of authors, ten are psychiatrists, two are psychologists, one is a social work professor, and one is a senior judge in the Family Division. It might appear that this is a book by psychiatrists for psychiatrists. The stated intention of the editors is that it ‘should be of interest to a spectrum of professionals involved in child welfare and family court work’. The reader is left in no doubt that this has been achieved and that the book stands well alone, without the earlier companion volume, as a current guide and reference book to best practice in assessment work by Mental Health professionals within family proceedings. Individual chapters on a particular topic also can stand alone, and some make a particularly distinguished contribution in the context of this excellent book.

Sections proceed from ‘Principles and practice’ through sections on ‘Children’, on ‘Parents’, on ‘Recommendations’ through to a final section on ‘Judgements’. Chapter headings are engaging, e.g.: ‘Would cultural matching ensure culturally competent assessments?’; ‘Does the past predict the future?’; ‘Are children reliable witnesses to their experience?’. These questions, and other chapter headings, are highly relevant to all varieties of clinical work. It is this wide relevance and high quality of content that redefines the book: it becomes of general interest, and not simply for specialists. The book is for all mental health professionals, including those in training, for child care workers and those working in family law, including lawyers, Guardians and CAFCASS officers. There is something of value for those at all levels of competence and experience: this is illustrated below by just three chapters.

Commentary by a child and adolescent psychotherapist trained at the British Association of Psychotherapists

Ann Horne

Ann Horne

48 Lynette Avenue
London SW4 9HD
UK

Ann Horne  

It is not easy - and sometimes feels presumptuous - to comment on a session in the middle of a therapy that has continued for a considerable time. Jane is not an easy child, neither for her carers nor for her therapist, and all of these adults should be

116

congratulated on having sustained such permanency for her, especially given her early life experience. It is, moreover, a very false situation: there is much more to Jane and to her therapy than one session can possibly indicate.

Preparatory thoughts from Jane's history

It is essential to keep in mind the trauma this child has suffered and how this might be enacted in the present and in the transference. Jane experienced ‘severe abuse and neglect’ in her family of origin. There was marital violence. In addition there are many ways in which Jane continued to be treated abusively by her mother at the ‘infrequent and poor’ contact visits. Such a history makes us alert to the developmental insult Jane must have suffered. Over the period when we would expect the healthy child, with a ‘good enough’ experience, to be developing an ego ideal, to be dealing with oedipal issues and resolution and to be in the early stages of superego development, Jane was faced with parents whose relationship seems dominated by the violence between them - they are unlikely therefore to have had the children in mind - and with a situation where identification either with an abused mother or a violent father seemed fraught options. An early experience of violence, especially at a pre-verbal, pre-representational stage, will have been overwhelming to the immature ego. Such children often cathect the body and do not move on from this readily. The body thus remains a recourse when the ego is further overwhelmed by external trauma. We should, therefore, expect acting out with the body - and, if we are Winnicottians, seek ways of according ‘positive value’ to it (Winnicott, 1963: 210). Moreover, we should also expect a heightened vulnerability in such a child: Khan's concept of cumulative trauma is highly relevant to the multiply abused children whom we see today (Khan, 1963). With a child like Jane we know from the start that she will have little of the protective membrane that other children develop (Parsons and Dermen, 1999: 330 - 6) and will experience the slightest of impingements as traumatic. This means care in our approach to interpretation and an acute awareness of our countertransference. Finally, there is the role that a perverse early experience will play: Jane's mother appears to have been unable to stop herself from responding to Jane with further abuse, and this will be felt in the transference. The child who depends on the body-self frequently replays the emotional experiences of early childhood in order, in part, to repeat the accompanying physiological responses. This involves what amounts to an addictive state in some children - addiction to the body's natural endorphins (and, I think, also to adrenaline), which are released prior to the actual re-enactment (Hale, 2004). The therapist needs to have this process, too, in mind, as well as to be aware of the expectation that adults will be abusive and corrupt.

Clinical Essay Prize. As is the 100th anniversary of the publication of two of Freud's famous papers - ‘Dora’ and ‘Three Essays on Sexuality’ - the Journal invites papers that examine the relevance of such early ideas to our current work and thinking.

Research Essay Prize. On any research topic which is of relevance to child psychotherapy.

The winning papers will be published in the Journal, as will any suitable runners-up. We are also hoping to arrange for the winning papers to be delivered as a public lecture. Entries will be judged by a panel to be appointed by the Editors.

[[RunningHead]]

Clinical Commentary

Clinical Material

Background

Jane is 8 years old. She has been looked after by the same carers, Julie and David, since she was 4 years old. She is to remain in their permanent care.

Jane is one of a large group of siblings who suffered severe abuse and neglect culminating in all but one child being removed from the mother's care. The children and their mother had been residing in accommodation, having fled from the father's many violent episodes towards the mother (though not the children). Contact with birth mother is infrequent and poor, with the social worker identifying the many ways in which Jane would be treated abusively by her mother.

Presenting Problems

At the time of assessment, when Jane was 5 years old, she presented with extensive difficulties relating to containment. Easily frustrated, Jane would frequently erupt into major outbursts of violence and aggression, which, due to being a danger to herself, would necessitate her being held physically. She would often wreck her room destroying her toys and other items she valued, while hitting out viciously at anyone who was close by. She was described as unable to play normally either with peers or with toys, and constantly clingy and demanding of attention. Her carers were exasperated and exhausted by their experience of being ‘drained’ by her. There were additional aspects of Jane's functioning I came to discover in that Jane had profound difficulty separating fantasy from reality. I learned her play was at that stage not a symbolic representation and expression of her states of mind or the struggles in her inner world, but rather activity in which fantasy was at times psychotically confused with reality. Moreover, it became apparent in sessions that Jane had severe difficulty in experiencing or perceiving me as separate from her, instead seeming to believe that either I magically knew what was in her mind, or vice versa, without it having to be communicated.

Session (last one before Easter break)

Jane to my surprise was in the waiting room with Julie, her foster-mother (Jane's foster-father James usually brought her). Jane was seated beside Julie at the small table. Julie was holding up a picture, which I realized Jane was copying. When I arrived, Julie straightaway ushered Jane towards me and she instantly came to me without, I noticed, insisting on a kiss and hug the way she does with James.

Commentary by Caroline Essenhigh, consultant child psychotherapist at East Ayrshire CAMHS, Scotland

It must be in the nature of such discussions to want more information, and this may be particularly so after reading this material to some extent because it is part of an ongoing assessment, but also because of the level of uncertainty for everyone shown in the background material. The parents want answers to their questions about Steven and are frightened of what they might hear; they are also very uncertain about what to do for the best, whether in terms of what help to accept or how to respond to Steven. Maggie is also afraid that they might have compounded his difficulties through responding the wrong way. The psychotherapist is uncertain about the nature of Steven's difficulties, what treatment modality might be best and about the parents’ ability to commit to ongoing work with Steven. The solution that is described hints at a compromise, a time-limited piece of work with several aims: to find out more about Steven, to try and engage the parents in parent work, to assess their ability to support Steven in therapy at a later date, if it is thought appropriate, and finally to help Maggie come to terms with Steven's difficulties. Maggie comes weekly but is seen jointly with Steven every other week. There was clearly a question about whether Steven should be seen at all during this time but he was included because of the fear that the parents would not attend without him also being seen. It would also ‘be easier' the therapist goes on to say, ‘to use what came up in joint sessions with Steven to help her think and reflect about difficulties, and to help her make more use of her individual sessions’. The father, Peter, would be seen every couple of months with Maggie.

A great deal of thought has gone into reaching this decision and I like the creative response to so many unknowns; however, it did seem a lot to manage, many different needs and tensions to keep in mind.

Commentary by Trudy Klauber, consultant child psychotherapist, Child and Family Department, Tavistock Clinic

It is easy to criticize parent work, just as it is extremely easy to criticize parents and parenting. It is all the more easy to criticize work with parents when there are so many versions of it and its primary task. The work is, in reality, extremely difficult, not least because it is not usually the direct psychotherapeutic encounter, which is the basis of

249

most of our training. In most of our therapeutic work, we think about and use the transference, more or less directly, depending on our theoretical orientation.

In this case, the work described is still in an exploratory phase, to be reviewed after 6 months of fortnightly work with mother (and sometimes father). These sessions alternate with fortnightly sessions when Steven comes with his mother. Decisions about organizing individual treatment for him are delayed by uncertainty about whether it will be beneficial, despite the fact that he has engaged well in individual assessment sessions. At this point, his mother's needs in relation to managing him and his behaviour seem paramount. There is also a fear that the parents might not engage in long-term parent work and would then stop bringing Steven. There are evident differences between mother and father in relation to the ‘mixed and unclear diagnostic picture’, and, even in the session described in detail, mother oscillates between a position that is in sharp contrast to father, and one in which ‘we’ are united, at least in rejecting the diagnosis of an autistic spectrum disorder.

Whatever the diagnosis might be, and there are several on offer, Steven is a boy who has been the source of great anxiety. There seems to have been a threat, at least in mother's mind, that he would react strongly to weaning; he certainly seems to have had difficulties in being able to sleep on his own at night, from 2 years old. The most obvious difficulty at that time, however, from the parents' point of view, was that his language was regressing. Additionally he could not accept ‘no’, and was full of rage if he didn't get what he wanted. Then they sought help over a period of 1ψ years from professionals whose diagnoses differed. The parents differed between themselves as well - father feeling there was something genetic on the paternal side of the family, linked with an idea of considerable ability.

Author biographies


 

Pamela Bartram trained as a child psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic having begun her clinical work as a music therapist. She currently works alongside non-CAMHS health professionals, assessing and treating the families of babies and pre-school children with disabilities such as those resulting from very premature birth and children on the autistic spectrum. She also has a role in the development and management of multi-disciplinary mental health services for children and young people with disabilities and their families. She is passionately interested in the impact of disability on mental health as well as the impact of mental health on disability.

Caroline Essenhigh currently works as Consultant child psychotherapist at East Ayrshire CAMHS in Scotland. She trained at the Anna Freud Centre where she continued to work until 2002. She has also worked in a children's home, as well as practising as a psychotherapist in a school for boys with emotional and behavioural difficulties. She has worked in Tier 2 community-based adolescent psychotherapy services, in both the NHS and the voluntary sector, and within a CAMHS service in east London. She also has a particular interest in working with learning disability as well as hard to engage cases such as conduct disordered children.

Lynette Hughes is an adult and couple psychotherapist, with a background in social work in child and adolescent mental health. She recently retired from the Winnicott Centre, Central Manchester and Manchester Children's Hospitals NHS Trust and is now in private practice. She worked previously in the Tavistock Marital Studies Institute and the Maudsley Hospital. She is particularly interested in the application of psychoanalytic ideas to the delivery of front-line services, and is the co-author, with Paul Pengelly, of Staff Supervision in a Turbulent Environment (1977, Jessica Kingsley).

Charlotte Jarvis is a Consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist, and Director of Open Door, Young People's Consultation Service, which is a charity based in the voluntary sector that provides a young people's psychotherapy service and a parent consultation service. Until recently she was the coordinator of a personality development course based in Leeds and Sheffield. She lectures occasionally on adolescence at the Tavistock Clinic, London, and recently at the Birmingham Trust for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy.

Child Psychotherapy: A Report from the Tavistock ClinicDilys Daws and Judith Loose (eds) Psychoanalytic Inquiry, 19(2). New Jersey: The Analytic Press, 1999159 pp., £12.00

Sheila Miller

Sheila Miller

Tavistock Clinic 120 Belsize Lane London NW3 5BA

Sheila Miller  

Psychoanalytic Inquiry is a ‘Topical Journal for Mental Health Professionals’, published in New Jersey, with a largely American readership. This volume is entitled, Child Psychotherapy: A report from the Tavistock Clinic. Child psychotherapy is not a recognized discrete profession in North America and dedicating a whole number to it and to the Tavistock is an interesting venture, secured, I surmise, by the goodwill established by Dilys Daws in her international contacts. She and her co-editor, Judith Green Loose, have collected a set of interesting and representative papers. These give a comprehensive view of the child psychotherapy training and the rich clinical, theoretical and applied work that has been developed by the graduates of the training which was established 50 years prior to the date of publication. Because of the success of this issue, extra copies have recently been reprinted.

When the journal was first published, I wondered, given my long working experience of the Tavistock training, if it would provide anything new; and then having found it rich and useful, feared I might be biased. As I was working in South Africa at the time, I was interested in the reaction of an audience who did not know at first hand the child psychotherapy training or indeed the Tavistock. The multidisciplinary groups in which we discussed some of the papers considered them inspiring and admired the way that complicated concepts were conveyed clearly and without resort to jargon. They found cause for hope in the accounts of the many small beginnings, which were nurtured into impressive developments.

Margaret Rustin's chapter on ‘Philosophy and practice’ puts the Tavistock training in the context of the development of the profession in the UK and details its history, noting all the important figures who developed the training. This should be of interest to current trainees as well as to practising therapists who might be familiar with the Tavistock of their training era, but to whom the perspective over 50 years would be new. Though offered in elegant and readable form, this is a deeply reflective consideration of the complexities involved in enabling professionals to manage the varied tasks now undertaken by the profession. Attention is devoted to defining the distinctive quality of the course and the institution in whose tradition it is embedded. Her respect for the importance of clinical work is expressed in the concluding paragraph: ‘this overview of the Tavistock training will only acquire resonance in the reader's mind when taken in conjunction with the clinical papers that follow’ (p. 140).

Clinical Material

Parent work: Background and presenting problems

Maggie and her husband, Peter, originally from the north of England, live with their son Steven, and his older brother, Mark, having moved to London when Mark was first born. There is a 4-year age gap between the two boys.

Steven was born during a time when Peter was becoming very successful and busy with his work, and was away from home a great deal. Maggie herself had given up a successful career in order to start a family, and was disappointed that Peter was away so much. Maggie remembers the pregnancy and birth as otherwise having been unproblematic.

There were no reported difficulties with Steven during his first 2 years. Steven was described as an easy baby, who didn't cry very much. He breastfed well, and moved easily onto solids by 6 months. Maggie weaned Steven gradually, until he was just breastfeeding at night, finally stopping altogether when he was nearly 2 years old. Steven did not seem to mind this particularly, but Maggie had been quite anxious, because they were already starting to have trouble with Steven's tantrums, and his sleeping difficulties (not wanting to go to bed, or waking up at night and wanting to return to the parental bed).

The parents first became concerned about Steven when he was about 2 years old. Having started to babble at 10 months, acquiring a few words by 18 months, Steven's language development seemed to regress. He no longer used the words he had already achieved, instead continuing to babble using nonsense words, making no attempt to string words together. Otherwise, however, both parents felt that he was extremely communicative non-verbally, able to indicate what he wanted. They felt that the ‘terrible twos’ were much more difficult with Steven than anything they had experienced with their older child. They both felt that Steven was like his Dad, unable to accept a ‘no’. Steven got into terrible rages when he could not get his own way. Maggie noted that Steven would interrupt any conversations or time she had with her older son, and that Steven always seemed to require the majority of her available time, energy and attention.

Research Digest

Infant observation as research: cross-disciplinary links

Maria RhodeJournal of Social Work Practice, November 2004, Volume 18, Number 3: 283-98

All abstracts are reproduced with the permission of the publishers.

Infant observation has long been an essential part of many clinical trainings, as well as a component of some academic courses in applied psychoanalysis, but its research potential is just beginning to be tapped. This paper reviews some of the literature on infant observation as a research method. This type of naturalistic observation is compared and contrasted with empirical research in the laboratory with regard to the results that may best be obtained by each method. Strategies for the retrieval of information from process recordings are discussed, and the importance of convergent findings from different lines of enquiry and of theoretical triangulation is considered. Observations illustrating language development are used as an example of the further dimension, which naturalistic observations can contribute to formulations deriving from clinical practice and empirical laboratory research. It is argued that convergences with psychoanalytic theory and with formulations from other disciplines, such as literary criticism, strengthen the confidence that may be accorded to formulations deriving from infant observation.

Risk-taking, dangerous behaviour in childhood: child protection and clinical strategies

Janet AndersonJournal of Social Work Practice, March 2004, Volume 18, Number 1: 19-32

This paper describes the findings of qualitative clinical research into risk-taking, dangerous behaviour in childhood using a post-Kleinian psychoanalytic approach undertaken by a child psychotherapist working in a local CAMHS. The purpose of the research was to find a way of understanding this behaviour using psychoanalytic thinking and comparing material from a number of cases across a wide age range (grouped into three age bands).

Editorial

Graham Shulman and Janine Sternberg

Janine Sternberg

Janine Sternberg  

This is a special edition on the theme of work with parents. It includes papers from three continents – with contributions from the UK, USA and Australia – and continues the trend of the Journal's increasing international character. The range of papers in this issue highlights both similarities and differences in style, emphasis and approach to work with parents – across different continents and between a variety of work settings. These articles prompt us to think again about the aims, methods and applications of psychoanalytically informed work with parents, and the nature of the engagement with parents that we offer. From a different perspective, the Clinical Commentary section is also on work with parents, and similarly prompts considerations of theoretical and technical issues in such work; here there is an added level of complexity in terms of work with parents of a child with an autistic spectrum diagnosis.

A notable feature of the articles in this edition is the recurrent reference to, and discussion of, the wider cultural context and its impact on parenting and hence on work with parents; we cannot read these papers without being struck by the parallel between the child's context of the family and the parents' context of the culture they are part of.

The opening paper, ‘Changing positions: helping parents look through the child's eyes', is by Pamela Sorensen, Assistant Professor of Psychiatric Medicine at the University of Virginia, USA and Director of the Under Fives Study Center in the Division of Child and Family Psychiatry. Sorensen, whose writing is lucid and compelling, delineates some of the ‘cultural impediments’ to parenting. Sorensen suggests that culturally determined ‘basic assumptions’ about children and child development can profoundly interfere with parents being able to understand the links between a child's behaviour and their emotional experience and relationships, i.e. ‘to look through the child's eyes’. Sorensen describes a non-clinical intervention called ‘parent education consultation’ that has been developed as an alternative to what she sees as the prevailing psychiatric or behavioural approach in America.

Asha Phillips  

We are told in the introduction that Jane has difficulty in experiencing being separate. This is apparent right from the start in the waiting room. The scene is set, Jane is copying a drawing, not creating one and she leaves her foster mother without saying goodbye. We can wonder whether she denies the separation or just does not feel separate? Once in the room it is as if the therapist then replicates Jane's feelings, Jane's ‘slopping down', the therapist's ‘sinking feeling’ and her later feeling of being invaded. There is clearly in work with this little girl a sense that the boundaries between people, the differences and/or similarities, are of great importance. I therefore look to the session to see where the therapist can give the child a taste of being with somebody else, of being interested in being with another, and of exploring the question of ‘Can you be together but separate?’

We can see by Jane's agenda ‘Now what shall I think about?’ that she has a sense of the kind of person the therapist is, somebody who is interested in thinking. There is some idea of separateness here. But the question seems also to be how can Jane be somebody who thinks?

Author biographies


 

Diana Cant is a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist with the Peper Harow Foundation and in private practice. She also acts as consultant to the staff teams at a number of CAMHS clinics in Kent. She has worked in several therapeutic communities, including 10 years at the Caldecott Community, and has a particular interest in residential work with severely damaged children. She is a visiting tutor on the adult psychotherapy training course at the University of Kent, teaching infant observation. She is also an external examiner at the Tavistock Clinic and at the University of Reading.

Ann Horne is a member of the BAP and SIHR and an Honorary Member of ČSPAP, the Czech Society for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy. She trained as a child and adolescent psychotherapist in the Independent tradition at the British Association of Psychotherapists where she served terms of office as head of the training and later of post-graduate development for child psychotherapists. She teaches and supervises at the BAP, Anna Freud Centre, SIHR and in Prague. Recently retired from the Portman Clinic in London, she has a particular interest in the child's use of the body in delinquency, abusing or seemingly seeking perverse solutions.

Angela Joyce formerly worked as a psychiatric social worker with ILEA. She then trained as a psychotherapist with the Guild of Psychotherapists and, subsequently as a psychoanalyst at the British Psychoanalytic Society and as a child analyst at the Anna Freud Centre. She has a particular interest in infancy and works as part of the Parent-Infant Project at the Anna Freud Centre. She taught child development there as an honorary lecturer with UCL for 8 years and now teaches mother – infant observation.

Jenny Kenrick is a consultant child psychotherapist teaching on clinical trainings at the Tavistock Clinic, BTPP and in Italy. Until recently she was co-convenor of the Fostering and Adoption Workshop and a member of the Fostering and Adoption Team at the Tavistock.

Valerie Sinason  

Literature and psychoanalysis have long been valued at the Tavistock Clinic. Martha Harris, the luminous child psychotherapist and psychoanalyst, who, with John Bowlby, founded the child psychotherapy training (from which six of the nine writers come), fought off yearly attempts to exclude the degree of English Literature as a satisfactory prerequisite for the training. There were calls for medicine, psychology and sociology to be the key background degrees. However, Mattie commented that being steeped in literature was a great bonus, something that her daughter Meg Harris Williams, who is quoted from extensively in this evocative book, fully understood. The current Head of the Child Psychotherapy Training, Margaret Rustin has followed in this tradition by writing extensively on children's literature together with her husband, Professor Michael Rustin.

Co-editors child psychotherapist Hamish Can-ham and poet/sociologist Carole Satyamurti chose the title Acquainted with the Night from a poem by Robert Frost. Among the feelings they hoped the title would evoke were awareness of death and the intensity of experience and feeling that the night can bring.

Tragically, Hamish Canham died in 2003 at the age of 41, before the book was finally published. He did, however, know it was almost within the public sphere. Carole Satyamurti, commenting on the new Hamish Canham Poetry Prize, established by his parents (Poetrynews, 2004), wrote movingly about his last days surrounded by his loving family. A few days before his death she read poems to him, focussing on Frost, Larkin and George Herbert: ‘… I will never forget his complete attention and stillness as I read. It renewed my sense that poetry - the sound and music of it, perhaps even more than the sense -has power to reach across the deepest chasms’.

Poetry and psychoanalysis reach profound issues of life and death. At the very start of psychoanalysis, Freud brought in his appreciation and ambivalence of the poet. For Freud, the poet delved deeper than the psychoanalyst and brought forth the fruits of the unconscious - the psychoanalyst could illuminate the meaning. At the beginning of one of the most brilliant psychoanalytic/literary amalgams, The White Hotel, D.M. Thomas (1981) speedily allows his fictional Freud to quote from A Midsummer Night's Dream that ‘the lunatic, the lover and the poet are of imagination all compact’.

Clinical commentary

Clinical material

Background

Peter is 6 years old and has been attending psychotherapy three times a week for 18 months. This takes place in a clinic context in which child psychotherapy is struggling to establish itself and due to problems within the service no ongoing work with parents is currently being offered, apart from the therapist meeting with the parents for reviews. When he was 2½ years old, Peter's baby sister died soon after birth from a non-treatable medical condition. His parents felt that they were emotionally unavailable for Peter at the time.

Peter was referred to the local Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service a couple of months after he started school at the age of 5. The parents described Peter as a physical, active and strong-willed baby and as a determined and stubborn young child. They felt that they adapted to his wishes and did not feel there were significant problems until he started school. He was physically aggressive to himself, to children, staff and particularly his parents. Peter was unable to concentrate and was described as ‘overactive’.

Although there is an occasional outburst in response to an unbearable emotional pain, physical aggression is no longer a major problem. He continues to need full-time, one-to-one support in school to support his attention to task and listening. Colleagues have discussed with his parents a possible diagnosis of ADHD. However, his parents do not want to pursue a diagnosis or use medication at this stage.

After months of repeatedly building and smashing up Lego in sessions, Peter came to view me as his persecutor and his fear, hatred and aggression were directed towards me. Following a period of a hide-and-seek game, Peter seemed to see me as a more benign and helpful figure, and this session comes at the beginning of a new stage of symbolic play.

Session

I went down to collect Peter and he was in the corridor getting a drink of water. Peter took a little drink, placed his cup on top of the water cooler and came through to the therapy room.

The Many Faces of Asperger's Syndrome

Maria Rhode and Trudy Klauber (eds)

London: The Tavistock Clinic Series, Karnac, 2004

302 pp., £18.99

Much has been written on the topic of autism ever since Kanner and Asperger, each unaware of the work of the other, independently published their clinical observations within a year of each other in 1943 and 1944, respectively. A most striking concomitant of their discoveries has been the degree of clinical interest in the condition, which has continued unabated ever since, despite modest levels of achievement in treating the condition. It cannot be without significance that children in whom there is such a strong aversion to personal contact should stimulate equally strong motivation in their parents and carers to overcome their resistance and restore that personal and uniquely human link, which provides emotional sustenance and satisfaction to both parties. This sustained effort to challenge individuals with autistic characteristics underscores philosophical and psychoanalytic convictions about the significance of primordial sharing experiences as the foundation for human evolution and personality development; the ‘you and I’ unit of personal relatedness (MacMurray, 1961).

It is the ‘you and I’ ‘unit that is scrutinised in the process of psychoanalysis, dependent on but more than, looking at “ways of being with the other” ’ (Fonagy, 1999). But psychoanalytic theory, as the exploratory tool for this method of treatment, is put to the test when one component of the unit is itself problematical. Psychoanalysis, by its very nature, requires the participation of the patient, and Bion has discussed the problem created for the analyst when the patient does not allow analytic work to be done. ‘Analysis is practically the only contractual arrangement between two people in which you feel you can keep on for ever – or for as long as you like – without anything ever happening’ (Bion, 2000). The psychoanalytic treatment of autistic conditions presents, therefore, a double challenge: one in relation to the inherently avoidant (and/or voiding) patient and the other in relation to the limitations of the analytic tool.

Author biographies

Andrew Briggs trained at the Tavistock Clinic. He is head of Child Psychotherapy in West Kent NHS and Social Care Trust. He has particular clinical interests in children with autistic spectrum difficulties and children looked after by the State. His other publications include a consultation to a children's home, the application of observational techniques to clinical work with a difficult to reach young boy, and he edited Surviving Space; Papers on Infant Observation (Karnac, 2002), a festschrift for Esther Bick.

Caroline Case trained as a child psychotherapist at the SIHR after a long career in art therapy. She works as a child psychotherapist in a Child and Family Mental Health Service in the NHS in Bristol as well as in private practice as an analytical art therapist. She has published widely on art therapy, including co-editing Working with Children in Art Therapy (Routledge, 1990) and being co-author of The Handbook of Art Therapy (Routledge, 1992), both with Tessa Dalley. Her new book, Imagining Animals: Art, Psychotherapy and Primitive States of Mind, was published this year (Routledge, 2005).

Editorial

Janine Sternberg and Graham Shulman

Graham Shulman

Graham Shulman  

This edition of the Journal of Child Psychotherapy contains a collection of articles which give a flavour of how wide-ranging the issues that currently preoccupy child psychotherapists are, and simultaneously show how, even in the most diverse settings, the work of child psychotherapists is informed and made possible by close attention to detail and to the countertransference. All our contributing authors, including those writing in our clinical commentary section, emphasise how much they learned about their patients and how they were better able to understand their internal worlds, by taking note of their countertransference, with particular attention to their somatic responses. As Caroline Owens, in her paper which opens this volume, points out, there is an ‘inevitability of disturbing and painful countertransference experiences in our work’, and we see here all the authors struggling to find ways of managing their feelings and then using them in the service of the patients.

The clinical work described in this volume shows the authors grappling with children who have been profoundly damaged – physically, mentally or both – by their life experiences. Owens movingly describes her work with a boy who had become quadriplegic following a tragic traffic accident. Always being acutely aware of how her contact with him was making her feel, she addresses the ways in which his physical limitations caused her to adapt her technique in sessions with him. We are presented with a vivid picture of how both Owens and her patient worked together. Her real human response to his current dilemma, and the events in the past that caused it, form a central point of the paper, and Owens bravely considers whether her tears in front of the patient aided or interfered with the psychotherapeutic work.

Many of the same issues are addressed in the paper that follows, in which Maria Pozzi describes her work with a severely disabled adolescent boy, Harry. This paper, entitled ‘Love at first sight’, also pays attention to the warmth, respect and care that many therapists feel for their patients. Harry's physical disabilities again led to the therapist having to make adaptations to ‘standard technique’, and Pozzi discusses how at times she was uncertain what Harry's requests for her to act on his behalf represented. She pays particular attention to Harry's attempts to get her to touch him in various ways and she tries to explore the meaning of this. Pozzi refers to the links between these two papers and raises questions about whether work with severely physically disabled young people poses particular challenges for child psychotherapists.

This paper aims to explore factors influencing the parenting of adolescents and investigate what constitutes a helpful therapeutic intervention for a parent whose adolescent refuses or fails to engage in therapeutic treatment. Adolescents in mind

David Trevatt

David Trevatt

David Trevatt  

Adolescence, authoritative parenting, brief consultation, separation, development

Adolescents in serious emotional difficulty are often unwilling to accept help from formal and statutory services. However, they remain a great worry to their parents, families and society as a whole. In this paper, I present the development of a model where the parents of adolescents are seen without the adolescent being referred. The adolescents themselves are occasionally present to help in the thinking about what they need from their parents and what they find unhelpful. They are not there to be engaged in therapy. Parents are encouraged to restore their authority and develop their role as parents appropriate to the new demands and needs of adolescents, who are held in mind by the therapist and are engaged indirectly through the work with their parents.

Moved to tears: Technical considerations and dilemmas encountered in working with a 13-year-old boy with acquired quadriplegia 1

Caroline Owens

Caroline Owens

Caroline Owens  

Body, countertransference, mindbody, movement, projection, projective identification, Corps, contre-transfert, “esprit-corps”, identification projective, mouvement, projection, Körper, Gegenübertragung, mindbody, Bewegung, Projektion, projektive Identifizierung, Parole chiave: corpo, controtranference, corpomente, movimento, proiezione, identificazione proiettiva

Abstract

This paper is about therapeutic work with David, a 13-year-old boy who, at the age of 5, was the victim of a hit-and-run road traffic accident resulting in quadriplegia. The circumstances leading to the accident and its sequelae reveal a particularly complex picture, which combines early emotional deprivation and trauma. Although cognitively intact and able to speak, David could not move. Yet he created movement in others through a desperate necessity, by communicating via the employment of extreme projective forces. The highly complex presentation of emotional, psychic and bodily damage in the child, and in particular, David's physical paralysis, has had a profound impact upon what I have come to think of as the ‘mindbody’ of the therapist. Winnicott has talked of the infant's ‘psyche/soma’. Here I want to extend the notion and consider the bodily impact of projections in particular and how these have a powerful emotional and physical resonance on the ‘mindbody’ of the therapist, especially in therapy with a young person whose body is damaged. In this paper, I consider technical challenges and dilemmas encountered in the work, including the complex interplay of transference/countertransference phenomena. This unusual presentation of a boy in extraordinary circumstances led to considerations of psychoanalytic method and interpretative activity, which may be viewed as being inspired by ‘emotional truthfulness’.2

Dans cet article, l'auteur raconte son travail thérapeutique auprès de David, âgé de 13 ans, qui à l'âge de 5 ans fut victime d'un accident de la circulation avec délit de fuite, accident qui le laissa tétraplégique. Les circonstances qui aboutirent à l'accident et à ses séquelles forment un tableau particulièrement complexe mettant en jeu des carences affectives précoces et des traumatismes. Bien que ses capacités cognitives ne fussent nullement atteintes et qu'il fut capable de parler, David ne pouvait pas bouger. Par l'urgence désespérée de son discours, transmise grâce à des projections extrêmement puissantes, il réussissait à susciter du mouvement chez ses interlocuteurs. La présence conjointe et extrêmement complexe de dommages affectifs, psychiques et corporels chez cet enfant – et notamment sa paralysie physique – eut un impact profond sur ce que l'auteur en vient à appeler l'“ esprit-corps ” du psychothérapeute. D. W. Winnicott a parlé du “ psyché-soma ” du jeune enfant. Dans son texte, l'auteur élargit cette notion, notamment pour prendre en considération l'impact corporel des projections, ainsi que leur résonance émotionnelle et physique massive sur l'“ esprit-corps ” du thérapeute, surtout lorsque son patient est une personne jeune dont le corps est endommagé. L'auteur explore les défis et dilemmes techniques rencontrés au cours de son travail, y compris le jeu complexe de phénomènes transférentiels et contre-transférentiels. Ce traitement, inhabituel, avec un garçon dans des circonstances sortant de l'extraordinaire soulève des questions concernant la méthodologie psychanalytique et l'activité interprétative, questions qui peuvent être considérées comme étant inspirées par la “ véracité émotionnelle ”.

Dieser Artikel ist über die therapeutische Arbeit mit David, einem 13-jährigen Jungen, der im Alter von 5 Jahren das Opfer eines Unfalls mit Fahrerflucht war, der zu einer Querschnittslähmung führte. Die Umstände, die zu dem Unfall führten und seine Folgen legen ein besonders komplexes Bild dar, das frühe Vernachlässigung und Trauma kombiniert. Obwohl David kognitiv intakt war und sprechen konnte, konnte er sich nicht bewegen. Doch schaffte er Bewegung aus verzweifelter Notwendigkeit in anderen, indem er mit mithilfe der Benutzung von extremen projektiven Kräften kommunizierte. Die höchst komplexe Präsentation von emotionalem, psychischem und körpelichem Schaden in dem Kind und insbesondere Davids körperliche Lähmung, hatte eine tiefe Auswirkung auf das, was ich nun den ‘mindbody’ (Gemütskörper) des Therapeuten nenne. Winnicott sprach vom Psyche/Soma des Babies. Hier möchte ich diesen Begriff ausweiten und besonders die köperliche Auswirkung der Projektionen betrachten und wie diese eine starke emotionale und physische Resonanz auf den ‘mindbody’ des Therapeutens haben, insbesondere in der Therapie mit einer jungen Person, deren Körper beschädigt ist. In diesem Artikel betrachte ich technische Herausforderungen und Dilemmas, denen man in dieser Arbeit begegnet, einschliesslich der komplexen Wechselwirkung von Übertragungs/ Gegenübertragungsphänomenen. Diese ungewöhnliche Behandlung mit einem Jungen in aussergewöhnlichen Umständen führten zu Überlegungen zur psychoanalytischen Methode undzur Deutungsaktivität, die von ‘emotionaler Wahrheit’ inspiriert wird

Riassunto: In questo articolo si parla del lavoro terapeutico con David, un bambino di 13 anni che, all'età di 5 anni, fu vittima di un incidente stradale che portò alla quadriplegia. Le circostanze che portarono all'incidente e la sua sequela rivelano un quadro particolarmente complesso, nel quale emerge un misto di deprivazione emotiva precoce e trauma. Sebbene David fosse abile cognitivamente e potesse parlare, egli non poteva muoversi. Eppure il bambino generava movimento negli altri attraverso una disperata necessità, comunicando con l'uso di estreme forze proiettive. Il presentarsi di un danno nel bambino altamente complesso nella sua dimensione emotiva, psichica e corporea, ed in particolare, la paralisi fisica di David, hanno avuto un profondo impatto su ciò che ho iniziato a pensare come il ‘corpomente’ del terapeuta. Winnicott ha parlato dello ‘psiche/soma’ del neonato. L'autrice vuole nell'articolo estendere la nozione e considerare l'impatto corporeo delle proiezioni e come queste abbiano una risonanza emotiva e fisica molto forte sul ‘corpomente’ del terapeuta, soprattutto nella terapia con un ragazzo giovane il cui corpo è stato danneggiato. Nell'articolo considero le sfide tecniche e i dilemmi incontrati nel lavoro, compreso il gioco complesso dei fenomeni transferali e controtransferali. Editorial

Janine Sternberg and Graham Shulman

Graham Shulman

Graham Shulman  

Thanks to the generous sponsorship of our publishers, Taylor & Francis, the Journal of Child Psychotherapy has inaugurated an Annual Essay Prize. This edition contains the winning paper, and future editions will feature other prize submissions. Diana Cant, the winner of the first Essay Prize, has written a paper describing her work with a child in a residential children's home. Cant delineates the progress of the work, the child's growing abilities and her move into foster care. As well as containing the careful and detailed case material that is, we believe, the hallmark of papers in the Journal, the paper also makes a strong case for close cooperation between the therapist and those in the child's extended network. In this way, Cant's clinical experience leads her to argue the need for changes in technique.

Jenny Kenrick's paper similarly encourages us to think about our technique when working with fostered and adopted children. After an overview of the literature about interpretation, Kenrick considers how the needs of fostered and adopted children may require an alteration in the way we frame our interpretations to them. By giving numerous vignettes which detail exactly what was said and the child's reaction to it, she helps the reader to truly grasp the subtleties of the points she is making.

At the centre of this edition, there is a collection of papers on the theme of imitation and identification. In what at first seemed to be a coincidence, two papers submitted to us addressed the same theoretical issues. It occurred to us that this might be a subject that was preoccupying therapists and influencing their work, and that it may be timely to have a ‘mini feature’ on the topic. Graham Shulman has revisited Gaddini's (1992) seminal paper ‘On imitation’. His close commentary enables those of us unfamiliar with the original to have a sense of its main points, but also opens up a discussion about some of its ambiguities and inconsistencies. This theoretical paper sets the scene for the subsequent two, which both look at the way in which the use of imitation can be seen as a positive development. Maria Rhode's paper ‘Mirroring, imitation, identification: the relevance of children's primitive mental states to the sense of self’, addresses differences between a more superficial type of imitation and imitative identifications that are in the service of development. Utilizing her extensive clinical experience with children on the autistic spectrum, she considers the particular difficulties that these children have in being able to take in, and thus identify with, an undamaged maternal object. Rhode draws on infant observation and clinical material to look closely at ways in which imitative behaviour can be seen and understood. We are privileged to read detailed accounts of her approach in the consulting room, together with the extremely sophisticated way that she understands the material.

Current concern in the Association of Child Psychotherapists with issues of evaluation, clinical effectiveness and outcome research makes the opportunity of reviewing these two books particularly timely. Though focused on work with adults they contain valuable information for child psychotherapists trying to get their heads around central issues.

Leuzinger-Bohleber and Target's book is based on a 3-day international conference held in Hamburg in 1999. The conference was particularly important because a major part of it was given over to presentations generated by the German Psychoanalytic Association's follow-up study of long-term effects of psychoanalytic treatment, the largest and most comprehensive European study to date. In a useful introductory chapter, the editors outline economic and social factors currently driving research into the effectiveness of psychoanalytic treatment. They point out that there is a tension between psychoanalytic researchers and clinicians, and that the research needs to reflect what is specific about psychoanalytic treatment. The chapter is well referenced and includes an interesting discussion of the pro and cons of qualitative and quantitative methods and the domains that they each map.

Thereafter the book is divided into four parts. Part I, ‘Long-term treatment in the context of contemporary discussions,’ is historical, philosophical and political. In an interesting, intelligent chapter, ‘What are the aims of psychoanalysis?’, Anna Ursula Dreher points to the complexity of defining treatment aims in psychoanalysis, showing how differences in what can be expected at termination have been affected historically by theoretical, technical and social factors. The question of what psychoanalysis is worth raises issues of value that cannot solely be explained in economic terms.

Robert Wallerstein, generally regarded as a pioneer in psychoanalytic research in the USA, outlines three generations of psychoanalytic research. According to Wallerstein, the first generation relied on clinicians' views on whether their patients had improved, with criteria unspecified before hand. The second generation includes Fonagy and Target's follow-up review of over 700 cases treated at the Anna Freud Clinic, and the German Psychoanalytic Association's study, to be described later on. Although these studies are retrospective, Wallerstein also includes here prospective individual case studies where individuals' progress is followed systematically against various pre-selected variables to shed more light on significant underlying processes. An important finding from this generation of research is that therapeutic effectiveness does not appear to depend on being ‘completely analysed’, and that conflicts underlying symptoms are not shattered or obliterated by psychoanalytic psychotherapy, but are better mastered or lose their destructive power or poignancy. The latter effect is known as the ‘Pfeiffer effect’ after the researcher who discovered it.

A little boy's use of his male child psychotherapist to help him understanda painful conundrum?

Andrew Briggs

Andrew Briggs

Andrew Briggs  

Absent father, Asperger's Syndrome, maternal object, ‘no-entry defence’, primary and secondary skin formation, self-harm, Automutilation, formation d'une peau primaire et secondaire, la défense “ interdit d'entrer ”, objet maternel, père absent, Abwesender Vater, Asperger Syndrom, Mütterliches Objekt, die Abwehr kein Zugang', primäre und sekundäre Hautbildung, Selbstverletzung, Parole chiave: assenza paterna, Sindrome di Asperger; oggetto materno, difesa di tipo ‘no-entry’, formazione della pelle primaria e secondaria, auto-distruzione

Abstract

The role of a child psychotherapist's gender is not often considered in terms of treatment outcome. This paper discusses how aspects of being a male child psychotherapist influenced the successful treatment of a very young boy with Asperger's Syndrome. The paper highlights how the nature of his very early relationship with his mother and the absence of his father were the basis of his difficulties resulting in that diagnosis. It shows that his desire to seize the opportunity of working with a male enabled him to understand his feelings about his father, why it was so difficult to want to be with him and not his mother, and why he could not be without her.

Le rôle joué par le sexe du psychothérapeute d'enfants dans les effets du traitement est rarement pris en compte. Dans cet article, l'auteur montre qu'à un certain niveau le fait d'être un psychothérapeute homme eut une influence sur la réussite de la thérapie d'un très jeune garçon présentant un syndrome d'Asperger. Selon l'auteur, la nature de la relation précoce entre ce petit garçon et sa mère, ainsi que l'absence de son père, étaient à l'origine des difficultés qui conduisirent à ce diagnostic. Il montre que le désir de l'enfant de se saisir de l'occasion ainsi offerte de travailler avec un homme lui permit de comprendre trois éléments essentiels : ses sentiments à l'égard de son père, la raison pour laquelle il lui était tellement difficile de vouloir être avec lui plutôt que de rester avec sa mère, et ce qui faisait qu'il ne pouvait pas se passer de celle-ci.

Die Rolle des Geschlechts des Kindertherapeuten wird nicht oft bezüglich des Behandlungsergebnis in Betracht bezogen. Dieser Artikel diskutiert, wie Aspekte dessen, ein männlicher Kindertherapeut zu sein, die erfolgreiche Behandlung eines sehr kleinen Jungen mit Asperger Syndrom beeinflussten. Der Artikel unterstreicht, wie die Art seiner frühen Beziehung zu seiner Mutter und die Abwesenheit seines Vaters die Grundlage seiner Schwierigkeiten bildeten, die zu dieser Diagnose führten. Es zeigt, dass sein Wunsch, die Gelegenheit zu ergreifen, mit einem Mann zu arbeiten, ihm ermöglichte, seine Gefühle seinem Vater gegenüber zu verstehen, warum es so schwierig war, mit ihm und nicht seiner Mutter sein zu wollen und warum er nicht ohne sie sein konnnte.

Riassunto: Il ruolo che gioca il sesso dello psicoterapeuta infantile non è solitamente considerato in relazione al risultato del trattamento. In questo articolo si discute come il fatto di avere un terapeuta maschile abbia influenzato per certi aspetti il risultato positivo del trattamento di un bambino molto piccolo che soffriva della Sindrome di Asperger. L'articolo illustra come la natura della sua primissima relazione con la madre e l'assenza del padre furono alla base delle sue difficoltà che portarono alla diagnosi. L'articolo mostra come il desiderio del bambino di lavorare con un terapeuta maschile gli ha permesso di capire i suoi sentimenti verso il padre, perché era così difficile voler restare con lui e lo stesso non succedeva con sua madre, e perché non poteva restare senza di lei.

Abstract

This paper presents primitive states of mind in an adopted child, which had been engendered by traumatic experiences in infancy and early childhood. Vignettes from her therapy illustrate difficulties in learning, speech and interaction, which were inhibiting her relationships with her adopted family from developing. The development of thought-images, comprehension of the past and representation of memory are explored through discussion of her play, painting and drawing in her relationship with her therapist.

Dans cet article, l'auteur explore, chez une enfant adoptée, les états psychiques archaïques engendrés par des vécus traumatiques dans sa petite enfance et au-delà. Des vignettes extraites de sa thérapie illustrent ses difficultés d'apprentissage, de parole et d'interaction relationnelle ; ces troubles entravaient tout approfondissement de ses relations avec les membres de sa famille adoptive. Le développement d'images-pensées, la compréhension de son histoire passée et la représentation de ses traces mnésiques sont explorés, au sein de la relation patient-thérapeute, à travers le jeu, la peinture et le dessin.

Dieser Artikel präsentiert primitive Gemütszustände in einem adoptierten Kind, die durch traumatische Erlebnisse als Baby und in der frühen Kindheit erzeugt wurden. Vignetten aus der Therapie illustrieren die Schwierigkeiten beim Lernen, der Sprache und Interaktion, die die Entwicklung seiner Beziehung mit der Adoptivfamilie einschränkten. Die Entwicklung von Gedankenbildern, das Verständnis der Vergangenheit und die Repräsentation des Gedächtnis werden durch sein Spiel, Malen und Zeichnungen in seiner Beziehung mit seiner Therapeutin exploriert.

Riassunto: L'articolo descrive stati mentali primitivi in una bambina adottata che soffrì di esperienze traumatiche nell'infanzia e nella prima fanciullezza. Vengono illustrate con il materiale clinico le difficoltà di apprendimento, linguaggio e interazione che inibivano lo sviluppo della relazione con la famiglia che l'aveva adottata. Lo sviluppo di immagini-pensiero, la comprensione del passato e la rappresentazione della memoria vengono illustrate attraverso la discussione del gioco e dei disegni prodotti all'interno della relazione con la terapeuta.

Correspondence

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards  

Dear Editors,

First of all, I would like to congratulate you on the success of the newly introduced Clinical Commentaries. While it had been a Journal aim for some considerable number of years, back to when Monica Lanyado and I were the editors, it had not actually been achieved, and it is very pleasing to be able to read such excellent material, with the appended commentaries, in what is hopefully now a regular feature.

The Commentary in the last Journal [31(2): 239 – 53] was to me of particular interest, and I found each clinician's careful suggestions on reading the sensitive work done by a therapist clearly under some pressure to provide a total package, which as they point out, is indeed a tall order, to be illuminating and in many ways complementary.

Pamela Bartram pointed up the difficulty parents may already have faced with ‘serial assessments’, and the importance of having a professional team working in conjunction rather than serially. This issue about resources and their particular uses, as she so rightly says, then leads the therapist to offer even more of herself – though in this situation it is indeed hard to know what else she might have done that would have felt helpful to the mother.

Caroline Essenhigh takes on the debate and talks of the inevitable levels of uncertainty, and the tension created in trying to address both child's and parents' needs, what she calls ‘the fine balancing act’ with which we are so familiar.

Trudy Klauber too takes up the difficulty of the framework in this case, the oscillations which occur in the parents' minds about differential diagnoses, and the resultant transference implications, which must also have a bearing on the reported feelings of mother about father's relative lack of presence in the day to day running of life at home. In a sense, the therapist is having to work too in a ‘single-parent’ role.

Several different suggestions are put forward about working with this case in terms of treatment frameworks. One which is not mentioned and which would I feel be invaluable, is the idea of family work, in this sort of case as a first-choice intervention. In my experience of setting up and running a family consultation centre for 7 years (Edwards and Maltby, 1998) initial work (usually time-limited rather than open-ended, which is in itself often reassuring to a family) with the whole family can be invaluable from a multiplicity of perspectives. It can offer the opportunity for a multi-professional approach, and this in itself can give other professionals something of the flavour of how a child psychotherapist's particular attention to play and its meaning can provide new thoughts both to workers and parents.

David Alcorn  

‘This important area of clinical practice’ is how Margaret Rustin describes ‘work with parents’ in her introduction to the EFPP clinical Monograph which carries that title (Rustin, 2000), and several remarkable papers in recent issues of the Journal of Child Psychotherapy (2003; Palacio Espasa, 2004) and elsewhere (Barrows, 2003) have confirmed that observation. Indeed, as Christine Frisch-Desmarez (2004) points out, ‘these new ideas emphasize in particular the impact of the family unconscious on child development and force us to re-think the individual treatment procedures used in the field of psychoanalytic psychotherapy’. Saralea Chazan's book, now in its second edition, is an important contribution to the discussion of the many questions raised by this kind of work - all the more so, perhaps, in that her approach is somewhat eclectic.

It is therefore probably better to begin by having as clear an idea as possible about what the author means by ‘simultaneous treatment of parent and child’; Chazan defines this in the first page of her Introduction as ‘the treatment of both members of a dyadic relationship, parent and child, separately by the same therapist’. Therein perhaps lies a problem… This, then, is no ordinary (and, nowadays, classic) approach in which a child has individual psychotherapy with his or her therapist, while the parents (both, if possible) are seen regularly or in parallel by the referring consultant or some other therapist - but in any case not the one who is working with the child. Nor is it the psychoanalytic ‘family therapy’ paradigm in which parents and child/children have treatment, as a family unit, in joint sessions with the same therapist. Nor again is it what Piovano (1998) calls ‘parallel’ treatment - child and parent(s) have separate sessions at the same time with two therapists who, at the end of each hour, meet to discuss relevant material.

The methodological difficulties to which Chazan's approach may give rise are briefly discussed by the author, though it is mainly through the extensive clinical material from the latter part of the book that considerations of confidentiality and transference/countertransference confusions come very much to the fore - and this despite the fact that, in the preliminary interviews, the author has explained to the child, as she puts it, ‘the meaning and limits of confidentiality’. Chazan does point out, however, that, in reality, it may not always be possible to have a second therapist working with the child's parents, however much we may think it desirable.

Surfacing the depths: thoughts on imitation, resonance and growth

Graham Music

Graham Music

Graham Music  

Imitation, resonance, attunement, child development, mirroring, mirror neurons

This paper examines some of the research on imitation that shows it to be much more than simply a behavioural or reflex response, but rather an aspect of the growth of genuine social and psychological interaction and part of an intersubjective process that includes the representation of object relationships. Differentiations between mind, behaviour and emotion may no longer stand up in the light of much of the new neuroscientific and other research of recent years, and the fact that thoughts and feelings have physiological and neuronal correlates. I will look at some of research about ‘mirror neurons’ as a way of trying to bridge such gaps. I will try to integrate some of these thoughts in an extended clinical example of a 4-year-old girl with some autistic features who was seen for intensive psychotherapy. In this I will examine the role of affect attunement, imitation, mirroring and the need to amplify emotional states as part emotional development.

Before the threshold: destruction, reparation and creativity in relation to the depressive position

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards  

Depressive position, reparation of self, paranoid-schizoid position and creativity, borderline and deprived children, Oedipal struggles, creative impulses and play, Enfants borderline et carencés, jeu et créativité, luttes œdipiennes, position dépressive, position schizo-paranoïde et créativité, réparation de soi-même, Depressive Position, Wiedergutmachung des Selbsts, paranoid-schizoide Position und Kreativität, Borderline und vernachlässigte Kinder: ödipale Konfliket, kreative Impulse und Spiel, Parole chiave: posizione depressiva, riparazione del sé, posizione schizo-paranoide e creatività, bambini deprivati e borderline, conflitto edipico, impulsi creativi e gioco

Abstract

In this paper, the author revisits the classic idea formulated by Hanna Segal that creativity takes place from a depressive position impulse to repair previous destruction wrought on internal parental objects. The author proposes that in the light of psychoanalytic work with deprived and borderline children, there may need to be a rider to this formulation. By suggesting the myths of Ariadne and Orpheus alongside that of Oedipus as aids to psychoanalytic understandings, a development is posited here which may coexist with or even precede depressive struggles. Dread and hope, the author suggests, accompany both the creative artist and the child on the path towards expression of creative impulses. Such impulses exist before a ‘depressive position’ arrival point, or may follow it, in a cyclical rather than linear development, as Britton – drawing on Bion – suggested. This does not diminish the importance of reparation both in the individual psyche and in creative work, but makes space for the possibility of a preceding or perhaps co-existing stage. Intimations of this were already present in the work of Melanie Klein, but were not elaborated in the way suggested here, as will be indicated. The author illustrates this with her own clinical work, and proposes that similar processes may be at work in the evolution of psychoanalytic understandings.

Dans cet article, l'auteur réexamine l'idée classique, formulée d'abord par Hanna Segal, selon laquelle la créativité prend sa source dans un mouvement psychique, lié à la position dépressive, qui vise à réparer des dommages infligés aux objets parentaux internes. Le traitement psychanalytique d'enfants carencés ou borderline conduit l'auteur à suggérer dans ce texte qu'il faudra peut-être modifier quelque peu ce postulat. En proposant comme appui à notre compréhension psychanalytique les mythes d'Ariane et d'Orphée en lien avec celui d'Œdipe, l'auteur suggère qu'un certain potentiel développemental peut coexister avec les luttes dépressives, voire les précéder. La terreur et l'espoir accompagnent aussi bien l'artiste dans son activité créatrice que l'enfant sur le chemin de l'expression de ses mouvements pulsionnels créateurs. Ces mouvements pulsionnels peuvent exister avant même d'atteindre la “ position dépressive ” ou peuvent accompagner celle-ci dans une trajectoire cyclique plutôt que linéaire, comme le suggère R. Britton à la suite des travaux de W. R. Bion. Cela ne diminue en rien l'importance de la réparation, que ce soit dans le psychisme du sujet ou dans le travail créatif quel qu'il soit ; cependant, un tel postulat ouvre un espace pour un stade qui précéderait la positon dépressive ou qui coexisterait avec elle. L'auteur montre que des indices d'une telle éventualité étaient déjà présents dans les travaux de Melanie Klein, bien qu'ils ne fussent pas élaborés de la même manière que dans cet article. L'auteur illustre ses propos par des exemples tirés de sa propre pratique clinique et suggère que des processus semblables sont peut-être à l'œuvre dans l'évolution de notre compréhension psychanalytique.

In diesem Artikel betrachtet die Autorin erneut die klassische, von Hanna Segal formulierte Idee, dass Kreativität von einem Impuls in der depressiven Position ausgeht, die vorherige Zerstörung, die den inneren elterlichen Objekten zugefügt wurde , wiedergutzumachen. Die Autorin schlägt vor, dass es angesichts der psychoanalytischen Arbeit mit vernachlässigten und Borderline Kindern eines Zusatz zu dieser Formulierung bedarf. Indem die Mythen von Ariadne und Orpheus neben denen von Ödipus als Hilfsmittel des psychoanalytischen Verstehens vorgeschlagen werden, wird hier eine Entwicklung postuliert, die mit depressiven Bemühungen koexistiert oder ihnen sogar voarusgeht. Furcht und Hoffnung, wie die Autorin vorschlägt, begleiten sowohl den kreativen Künstler wie auch das Kind auf dem Weg zum Ausdruck von kreativen Impulsen. Solche Impulse existieren vor dem Ankunftspunkt der depressiven Position oder können ihr auch in einer zyklischen statt einer linearen Entwicklung folgen, wie Britton mit Bezug auf Bion vorschlug. Dies vermindert nicht die Bedeutung von Wiedergutmachung sowohl in der individuellen Psyche als auch in der kreativen Arbeit, aber es eröffnet Raum für die Möglichkeit eines ursprünglicheren oder koexistierendem Zustands. Andeutungen davon waren bereits in den Schriften von Melanie Klein präsent, aber sie waren nicht in der Art und Weise ausgearbeitet wie das hier gezeigt werden wird. Die Autorin illustriert dies mit ihrer eigenen klinischen Arbeit und schlägt vor, dass ähnliche Prozesse in der Evolution des psychoanalytischen Verständnis stattfinden können.

Riassunto: In questo articolo l'autrice rivisita l'idea classica formulata da Hanna Segal secondo la quale il processo creativo nascerebbe dall'impulso nella posizione depressiva a riparare gli oggetti genitoriali interni precedentemente distrutti.L'autrice propone che alla luce del lavoro psicoanalitico con bambini deprivati e con bambini borderline, bisognerebbe introdurre una clausola a questa formulazione. Prendendo spunto dai miti di Ariadne e Orfeo oltre a quello di Edipo per facilitare la comprensione psicoanalitica, se ne trae che insieme o anche prima dei conflitti depressivi ci sia stato un certo sviluppo. L'autrice suggerisce che il terrore e la speranza accompagnano sia l'artista creativo che il bambino sulla strada verso l'espressione degli impulsi creativi. Questi impulsi esistono prima di arrivare alla fine della ‘posizione depressiva’, o possono seguirla, in un processo di sviluppo pi[ugrave] ciclico che non lineare come suggerisce Britton, rifacendosi a Bion.Tutto questo non sminuisce l'importanza del processo di riparazione sia per la psiche individuale che per il lavoro creativo, ma dà spazio alla possibilità di uno stadio precedente o forse coesistente. Indicazioni di questo erano già presenti nel lavoro di Melanie Klein ma non furono elaborate come si spiega nell'articolo. L'autrice illustra questo concetto attraverso il suo lavoro clinico e propone che processi simili avvengano nell'evoluzione della comprensione psicoanalitica.

This article describes a type of intervention with parents that attempts to stimulate and encourage empathic imagination in relation to their child's difficult behaviour.
